deep.reconstruction:
There are no mathematical derivations on this page. It is a philosophical and terminological note. It belongs to the 'Naturphilosophie (Neue Theorie)' material whose previous page sets out Gauss-type least-constraint molecular mechanics.

(1) The bracketed note ends with a red marginal instruction, 'Note unter dem Text' (to be printed as a footnote). Its first line ends a sentence: the aim is not to go back, as Leibniz or Spinoza did, to beings with a multiplicity of properties, but to reduce things to first grounds of the greatest possible simplicity. Riemann then discusses vocabulary. German renders Latin 'actio' as 'Wirkung', a word usually meaning 'effectus'. This makes phrases such as 'actio aequalis est reactioni' (Newton's third law) and 'principium actionis minimae' (least action) unclear. Kant got round this by adding 'actio, actio mutua' in parentheses after 'Wirkung, Wechselwirkung'. Riemann tries out German alternatives: 'die Kraft ist gleich der Gegenkraft' and 'Satz vom kleinsten Kraftaufwande'. He concludes that German lacks a word for 'agere', a striving directed at something else, and so he will use the foreign word.

(2) A note on the word 'Hypothese'. Today the word means anything added in thought to the phenomena, which is not Newton's sense. Newton was far from the absurd idea that explanation could be obtained by abstraction alone.
- Riemann quotes Newton's General Scholium: 'Et haec de deo ... Hypotheses non fingo. Quicquid enim ex Phaenomenis non deducitur, Hypothesis vocanda est.' His reading 'ad philosophiam experimentalem' matches the 2nd edition (1713); the 3rd edition (1726) reads 'naturalem'.
- He quotes Arago, Oeuvres complètes vol. 3, p. 505 (the Laplace notice): 'Une fois, une seule fois Laplace s'élança dans la région des conjectures ... une cosmogonie'. This refers to the nebular hypothesis; Riemann leaves out Arago's clause comparing Laplace with Kepler, Descartes, Leibniz and Buffon.
- He adds the Laplace–Napoleon anecdote: 'Sire, je n'avais pas besoin de cette hypothèse.'

(3) Riemann's own position: Newton's distinction between laws of motion (axioms) and hypotheses is untenable. The law of inertia is itself a hypothesis: a material point alone in the world, moving with a given velocity, would keep that velocity forever. In modern notation this is the counterfactual claim that m x'' = 0 for an isolated point, so x(t) = x0 + v t. The next page continues this: inertia cannot be derived from the principle of sufficient reason and needs a cause in the inner state of matter.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics on the page.
Minor: Arago is quoted with an ellipsis that is not marked; the original reads 'Laplace s'élança, à la manière de Kepler, de Descartes, de Leibnitz, de Buffon, dans la région des conjectures'.
The Newton quotation uses the 2nd-edition reading 'experimentalem'. This is accurate to that edition, but it differs from the better-known 3rd edition ('naturalem').

results.what: The law of inertia is a hypothesis, i.e. an empirical or counterfactual assumption about an isolated point, not an a priori axiom. Newton's split between axioms and hypotheses is rejected.
results.modern_name: Conventionalist/empiricist critique of the status of Newton's first law (cf. later Mach, Poincaré, Neumann's 'Body Alpha')
results.usually_credited_to: C. Neumann (1870), E. Mach (1883), H. Poincaré (1902) for prominent versions; it was also a long-standing philosophical theme

results.what: Terminological remark on rendering 'actio' (third law, least-action principle) in German.
results.modern_name: Terminology of action/reaction and the principle of least action

results.what: Historical quotations: Newton's 'Hypotheses non fingo', Arago on Laplace's cosmogony, Laplace's 'je n'avais pas besoin de cette hypothèse'.
results.modern_name: Standard quotations from the history of science

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds philosophical and terminological notes and standard quotations, with no mathematics. As far as I recall, this naturphilosophische material, including the remark that the law of inertia is a hypothesis, was published from the Nachlass in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (fragments of philosophical content). It is therefore known as his.

checkable.sympy: t,m,x0,v=symbols('t m x0 v'); x=x0+v*t; simplify(m*diff(x,t,2))==0
checkable.asserts: Uniform rectilinear motion x = x0 + v t satisfies the force-free equation m x'' = 0. This is the content of the inertia hypothesis for an isolated point.

checkable.sympy: t,x0,v=symbols('t x0 v'); x=Function('x'); dsolve(Eq(diff(x(t),t,2),0), x(t), ics={x(0):x0, diff(x(t),t).subs(t,0):v})
checkable.asserts: The unique solution of x'' = 0 with x(0)=x0 and x'(0)=v is x = x0 + v t: the velocity is kept forever.

transcription_corrections: 'Da aber in der That bei[?] ein eigener Ausdruck' — the word read as 'bei' is doubtful. The image seems to read 'Da aber in der That ein eigener Ausdruck für agere ... fehlt'; 'bei' is probably spurious, or possibly an abbreviation for 'uns'.
The Newton quotation in the manuscript has '&' (rendered 'et') before 'Hypotheses non fingo'. 'philosophiam experimentalem' is correctly read and is the 2nd-edition wording.
'Eigenschaften[?]' in the first line is plausible but uncertain; the word is badly faded.
'Arago, Oeuvres complètes T. 3. 505' is confirmed as the reference to Arago's notice on Laplace (Notices biographiques, vol. 3).
In 'zwischen Bewegungsgesetzen ... oder Axiomen', a short word after 'Bewegungsgesetzen' is struck out and illegible; the reading 'Bewegungsgesetzen' itself appears correct.
